question: A finance director asks why the team is proposing a smaller, faster Claude model for a high-volume invoice classification workflow instead of the most capable model available. What is the best way to justify this choice?
options: A) Explain that the most capable model cannot process invoices at all, so a smaller model is the only technically possible option.
B) Explain that classification is a straightforward task, so a faster and cheaper model can meet accuracy needs at lower cost and latency.
C) Explain that model choice has no effect on cost, so picking the smaller model is purely a matter of team preference.
D) Explain that smaller models are always more accurate than larger models for every business task the company might have.
correct_answers: B) Explain that classification is a straightforward task, so a faster and cheaper model can meet accuracy needs at lower cost and latency.
explanations: Incorrect. The most capable model can process invoices; it is simply not the most cost- or latency-efficient choice for this task.

Correct. For high-volume, relatively simple tasks like classification, a faster and cheaper model often delivers sufficient accuracy while reducing cost and latency, which is the standard model-selection tradeoff to communicate.
Incorrect. Model choice directly affects per-token cost and response speed, so it is not merely a matter of preference.
Incorrect. Smaller models are not universally more accurate; capability, task complexity, and cost must be weighed case by case.
